practice.title: Supercharging Practice with the Promise
agreedSteps: Continue working on your chosen delusion, but add a sense of promise — remember 'I promised to become enlightened for the benefit of all beings' and let that vow motivate and supercharge your practice.
Get familiar with the bodhisattva vows — read through the 18 root and 46 secondary downfalls in The Bodhisattva Vow and start learning what they are.
steps: Connect the delusion practice to benefiting others: when envisioning freedom from a delusion, include the capability to help others as part of that vision — not just personal improvement.
Use the vows as a decision-making framework: when facing a choice or fork in the day, try routing through any vows you know rather than reasoning from scratch.
Notice where specific vows don't make sense or feel resistive — that gap is the distance between you and the bodhisattva's way of life. Sit with it as a contemplation, not a judgment.
practice.quote: What we're looking at now is it's not separate from our practice of overcoming or conquering our delusions. Basically the way to do it is to become [a] bodhisattva and follow the bodhisattva's way of life.

commentary.title: The Snowball Effect of Real Practice
content: When we really go for a practice, it snowballs in a virtuous way. It doesn't matter what that practice is particularly — if we really go for it, naturally it spreads out into everything else that we're doing. There are systemic effects, chain reaction kind of effects that spread throughout the whole system of our mind.

Distraction is a particularly powerful delusion to focus on, because it becomes a blocker for every other type of virtue and is the highway to every delusion. Distraction is defined as a mind that wanders to an object of delusion. Every delusion is precipitated by distraction. So if you oppose distraction, you are blocking the highway to every other delusion.

commentary.title: Envisioning Freedom: Attachment vs. Tantric Imputation
content: When we envision freedom from a delusion, there are two very different ways to do it. If we're doing it with attachment — relating to some idealized version of ourselves as an inherently existent person who we are not — that's just going to be agitating. An inherently existent person is unrelated to us. So envisioning that inherently perfect self will feel like someone we can never become. That's just unrealistic expectations.

The correct practice is very different: we're thinking, this is who I'm going to become. In Tantra, we impute I on that person. By doing that, we start to feel like that's who we are and that's our potential, and then it feels very inspiring and uplifting. If we notice the agitation coming, it's because we're relating to this envisioned person as unrelated to us — as inherently existent — rather than as our own potential.
commentary.quote: This practice is very different because we're thinking, this is who I'm going to become. And actually when we do it, we think, this is me.

commentary.title: Catching the Absence: Proof Delusions Are Not Us
content: When we catch the moments that a delusion is not present, it's a proof that it's not inherently us. That proof is an essential part of the equation that will eliminate the delusion. It's not until we internalize that they're related but not one with us that we can make progress. It's the salt in the water, the dirt in the gold nugget, the clouds in the sky.

There's an intellectual understanding that delusion is not me — but there's a feeling to it that is a spiritual experience. When we get the right feeling of that truth, we almost feel like we can become liberated today. We feel utterly different from the delusions. If we don't feel that way with the contemplation, we should work on it more. The point is simple: catch when it's not there, therefore it's not one with me. Keep doing it over and over.
commentary.quote: The experience of it is a spiritual experience, where we feel like I am going to become enlightened in this life, because the delusion is not me.

commentary.title: Our Working Image of Freedom Is Probably Wrong
content: Our generic mental image of freedom from a delusion is often woefully inaccurate. If we go through all 26 delusions in How to Understand the Mind, we'll probably find that our version 1 is cosmically wrong, version 2 is still massively off, and version 3 is getting in the right direction but still not the experience.

This is incredibly helpful, because we realize: my whole practice is about uprooting delusions, but my working image of what that looks like isn't it. How many of us, when we work on attachment, think the answer is having less stuff? 100% wrong. Or when we think about abandoning anger, we envision passivity — not responding to things? The response has nothing to do with being angry or not. Not responding doesn't mean we've dealt with anger at all.

This actually encourages us. If we can't get a clear image and think, no surprise I've been having trouble — I don't even know what I'm aiming for — that's a huge moment. We're finally moving in the right direction.

commentary.title: Laziness: The Delusion Behind Not Enjoying Virtue
content: When we do something virtuous but we're not happy doing it, the mental factor laziness is occurring. It's a secondary delusion — a mind that prevents us from delighting in virtue. There are three kinds: the laziness of being attached to what's meaningless and non-virtuous, the laziness of discouragement, and the laziness of procrastination.

Freedom from the first laziness is contentment. Freedom from the laziness of discouragement is a deeply encouraged state that believes we can change and grow. Freedom from procrastination is a mind that understands the value of virtue so clearly that it would think — why would I wait to create causes of happiness? You wouldn't wait on a great investment tip. The procrastination comes from not truly believing that virtue is going to lead to good results.

commentary.title: Animal Mind vs. Human Mind
content: If we do nothing but engage in the usual self-cherishing thoughts, we're not much different from animals. Even birds and insects go from here to there trying to search for happiness and relieve their suffering. The label 'animal mind' is useful for our delusions — a lot of our attachment and need for security and validation are just tribal little animal minds, not elevated human minds or spiritual minds.

Real human life is a spiritual life. Otherwise we're living an animal life in a human body — like the Milarepa quote to Gampo Dorje: 'You have a human body, but an animal mind.' Once we label the delusions this way, we realize they're not clever, erudite, scholarly thoughts. They're just base pack minds. It helps us not buy into them so much.

commentary.title: Why Vows Are Necessary to Attain Enlightenment
content: There is no Buddhahood outside of taking vows. The vow is what bootstraps the experience. Between wanting to develop dharma minds and having developed them incontrovertibly, the vow is what bridges that gap. In between, we don't have the moral fiber and strength to just be at the destination — there's a conflict in the mind, delusions pulling in the other direction.

It's like a climber on El Capitan putting in pitons. The piton catches you if you fall — you don't fall the whole way down, only a certain amount. Without the piton — without the vow — when you fall, you fall all the way. So the vow is the protection that makes the climb possible in the first place.

Taking the vow also creates a special karma: we're constantly practicing the perfection of moral discipline as long as we have the vows on our continuum, which is a huge amount of merit. And the vow provides clarity — no conflicting desires, no tussling options. If it's up for grabs, it's very easy to compromise, and with delusions, once you compromise a little, you compromise a lot.
commentary.quote: [The] vow is what kind of like bootstraps the experience. [...] It's like a climber who's climbing up a huge rock wall [...] The climber puts in a piece of metal right into the wall to hold them from falling back [...] I might fall back to this point, but I'm not going below that.

commentary.title: Vows as Decision-Making Scaffolding
content: Life is full of split-second decisions, and if we try to figure out what to do starting from zero, there's often not enough mental space. By the time we've gotten somewhere on the decision, it's too late and we've got to act. The vows — refuge vows nested outside, bodhisattva vows within, tantric vows within those — give our mind something to route through when making decisions. We're never starting from scratch.

The 64 vows cover a lot of the situations we run into in life. With whatever mental energy we have, we're already starting from the bodhisattva's perspective on the matter, and we get to spend our energy figuring out the best way to handle it — instead of reasoning from ground zero. Over time, the vows become the structure of our mind. That's how we process things and navigate our life.
